claims.text: The proposed material is a Pt–Ru high-entropy-alloy nanomaterial produced by spray-drying followed by thermal decomposition-reduction.
The initial spray-dried nanopowders are disordered and have a non-uniform phase distribution.
The Pt–Ru ratio and secondary-heating conditions govern the kinetics of nanoframework phase evolution.
Increasing Ru content accelerates transformation from a disordered precursor into an ordered HEA nanoframe.
An ordered HEA nanoframe provides a more uniform distribution of active sites.
A more uniform distribution of active sites enhances catalytic performance.
Processing under an inert atmosphere prevents oxidation.
A suitable secondary-heating window can permit phase transformation without causing sintering.
Higher Ru content lowers the activation barrier for structural reordering during secondary heating.
Lowering the reordering barrier produces faster and more complete formation of an ordered nanoframe.
The resulting ordered nanoframe maintains high surface area.
Improved nanoframe structure enhances electron-transfer properties and catalytic-site accessibility.
Enhanced electron transfer and site accessibility increase catalytic performance in oxidation reactions.
Higher-Ru samples receiving optimized secondary heating will have greater phase uniformity and a more defined HEA nanoframework than lower-Ru or non-optimized baseline samples.
Higher-Ru, optimized-heating samples will exhibit higher turnover frequency or conversion rate than the baseline.
The proposed relationship is limited to spray-drying/thermal decomposition-reduction under inert atmosphere and a thermal window that avoids sintering or degradation.
The quantitative Ru-content threshold and optimal secondary-heating temperature and duration are unknown.
The extent to which the proposed structural changes directly improve catalytic kinetics remains to be empirically validated.
Sharper XRD peaks and uniform nanoframe morphology are indicators of improved phase ordering.

Failure to obtain statistically significant improvements in both ordering and catalytic performance relative to the baseline, or superior activity from a different structure, would falsify the hypothesis.
